records.text: Prosecutorial Misconduct Prosecutorial Witness Coaching / Testimonial Tailoring Evidence: Lauren Deal’s speech patterns and substantive framing changed materially between her law-enforcement interviews and trial testimony. Those changes align with testimony that the prosecutor suggested narrative revisions tied to witness fear. Legal Standard Violated: Napue v. Illinois ; due process Napue Witness Coaching Prosecutorial Evidence Authentication Failure Evidence: Facebook messages identified as Exhibit 4 were presented without device metadata, custodial proof, or other foundational evidence sufficient to resolve the exhibit’s attribution problem, particularly where later screenshots identified another user of the phone. Legal Standard Violated: N.C. R. Evid. 901(a); Rule 104(b) Authentication Foundation Failure Prosecutorial Violation of Conditional Admission Limits Evidence: The court indicated Exhibit 4 was admissible only if the State linked it to the prior conversation to provide context. That foundational condition was not meaningfully satisfied, yet the State proceeded as though the condition had been met. Legal Standard Violated: N.C. R. Evid. 104(b); due process fairness concerns Rule 104(b) Conditional Admission Prosecutorial Rule of Completeness Violation Evidence: Only the first screenshot of the Facebook exchange was emphasized, while additional screenshots identifying another phone user were excluded from the State’s presentation, creating a misleading impression of authorship and continuity. Legal Standard Violated: N.C. R. Evid. 106 Rule 106 Misleading Sequence Prosecutorial Aggravating-Factor Manufacturing Evidence: The “position of trust” theory hardened only after testimony and framing evolved well beyond the initial statements and objective video context. The record supports an inference that the aggravator was constructed rather than organically supported. Legal Standard Violated: Due process; Brady ; Napue Aggravator Narrative Construction Prosecutorial Retaliatory Charging Pressure Evidence: Aggravating exposure increased after plea refusal, supporting the inference that charging leverage was used coercively rather than neutrally. Legal Standard Violated: Due process; prosecutorial ethics Retaliation Coercion Prosecutorial Misrepresentation of Forensic Evidence Evidence: The State’s presentation of forensic evidence materially affected defense strategy and was framed in a manner the defense contends was inaccurate, incomplete, or misleading. Legal Standard Violated: Brady ; due process; professional ethics Forensic Misconduct Prejudice Prosecutorial Shifting Injury Claims: Three Incompatible Accounts Evidence: Deal’s injury account evolved materially across three stages. The State presented each version without accounting for the prior contradictions. Freeman corrected his own in-court testimony after a lunch recess — changing where and when he observed injuries — suggesting the matter had been addressed during the break. Stage 1 — Deal to Officer Haines (recorded interview) “I have bruises on my arms from being held down. They took pictures of them at the hospital. They took a lot of pictures at the hospital.” Stage 2 — Freeman corrects his own testimony after recess Cruz: “I didn’t see that in the video. Was that in the video?” Freeman: “When she got there.” Cruz: “So prior to the interview?” Freeman: “Yeah, as we were going back.” [After lunch, Freeman returns to the stand and reverses this answer.] Cruz: “So this happened after the interview?” Freeman: “Yes.” Stage 3 — Deal at trial “Maybe a bruise on the front of her arm from when she got pushed down… that bruise may have come from falling in the woods.” No wrist bruises claimed. No hospital photographs referenced. No such photographs exist. On cross-examination, Haines confirmed Deal had told him the bruises were from being “held down” around the wrist — a claim Deal abandoned entirely at trial. Freeman continued to assert wrist injuries even after Deal had retracted that account. Legal Standard Violated: Napue v. Illinois ; Giglio v. United States ; duty not to present testimony the State knows to be inconsistent with the evidence Napue / Giglio Injury Contradiction Corrected Testimony Prosecutorial Facebook Exhibit: Judge’s Foundation Requirement Not Satisfied Evidence: State’s Exhibit 4 — a December 3, 2016 Facebook message — was conditionally admitted over defense objection. Defense counsel noted the exhibit’s own pages identify the sender as “Matt” using the defendant’s phone, and that the defendant himself states at the end that he did not have possession of his phone. The court admitted only the first page, conditioned on the State supplying testimony of a prior conversation before 1:49 p.m. that day. The State never elicited that testimony. Wunsch objection (trial record) “In this message, it clearly states — I mean, she is picking out part of it, but in this message, it clearly states that this is not Ben. It’s Matt. I’m using his phone… at the very end, Ben comes on, identified himself, saying, I didn’t have my phone. I’m sorry.” The Court’s condition for admission “If she testifies that they had a discussion prior to December 3, 2016, at 1:49, then that would give this particular page context… they will need to link this up with a conversation prior to December 3, 2016.” Bartholomew did not ask Deal whether she and the defendant had discussed the bonfire before 1:49 p.m. Having Deal read a text that says “Remember when I said I was having that bonfire…” is not independent testimony that the prior conversation occurred. The exhibit was introduced to support an aggravating factor — special position of trust — founded on a three-year-old partial screenshot in which the identified sender is disputed by the exhibit’s own content. Legal Standard Violated: N.C. R. Evid. 901; R. Evid. 106 (rule of completeness); due process; conditional admission obligations Authentication Failure Rule 901 / 106 Aggravating Factor

records.text: Investigative & Prosecutorial Misconduct Framework Investigation Investigative Phase Failures Confirmation Bias: The case appears to have been escalated before the factual predicate was fully developed, suggesting a theory-first rather than evidence-first investigation. Selective Witnessing: Narrative-supporting witnesses were prioritized, while potentially exculpatory witnesses were not meaningfully pursued. Conflict of Interest: Familial and relational ties created, at a minimum, an appearance of compromised neutrality. Chronology Instability: Key reports and testimony do not align cleanly on when the detective became involved or how probable cause was formed. Bias Suppression Timeline Prosecution Prosecutorial Strategy Patterns Narrative Reconstruction: Trial testimony evolved in ways that cured weaknesses in the original account. Aggravator Expansion: Social familiarity was reframed into a more legally useful “position of trust” theory. Evidence Framing: The State relied on exhibits and theories that were presented more forcefully than they were grounded. Pressure Tactics: Increased exposure after plea refusal supports an inference of coercive leverage. Strategic Omission: Inconsistent or weakening material was not treated with the candor required of a minister of justice. Strategy Fabrication Omission Testimony Testimonial Fabrication Indicators Progressive Elaboration: Details multiplied over time, mapping neatly onto legal elements. Linguistic Shift: Content words changed more than function words, suggesting retraining rather than organic memory continuity. Retroactive Insertion: Themes such as fear, trust, freezing, and witness-related terror emerged more strongly at trial than in earlier accounts. Contradiction Cascade: Later details created tension with video, chronology, physical plausibility, and witness interviews. Disregard of Objective Video Evidence: Testimony proceeded as though surveillance video would not materially challenge the narrative. Fabrication Credibility Coaching Judicial Judicial Oversight Failures Authentication Relaxed: Evidence was allowed in despite unresolved foundation problems. Conditional Limits Not Enforced: The State proceeded beyond the court’s own qualification regarding admissibility. Lack of Enforcement: No meaningful corrective response appears to have followed despite repeated reliability concerns. Judicial Oversight Evidentiary Failure

On this page ➜ Linguistic Analysis Cognitive Rationalizations Investigative Physical Plausibility Prosecutorial Constitutional Linguistic Witness Construction Forensic linguistic analysis compares the complainant's 2019 initial statements to her 2023 trial testimony. The sharp drop in cosine similarity from the baseline reflects a shift from situational recall to legalistic element-filling — suddenly claiming she “froze,” suddenly invoking fear of witnesses — aligning with sworn testimony that ADA Bartholomew coached her in the courthouse lobby before trial. Cosine Similarity of content words. Score of 1.0 = Perfect Match. Score of 0.28 = Heavily Engineered. ✖ The “Lobby Coaching” Incident Sworn Testimony (Steven Happel, Tr. 112): “I heard Ms. Bartholomew tell the victim that she should have said that the victim was afraid of the witnesses… I felt like my thought process was trying to be played with.” ✖ The Suppressed $150k Extortion A third party who is friends with the complainant attempted to extort $150,000 from Allen to “drop the charges.” The defendant’s attorney received the information but never investigated it. ⚖ Falsification of the Verdict Record After the jury foreperson read the 12‑0 acquittal on First-Degree Rape into the record, ADA Bartholomew filed “Findings of Fact” that scrubbed the acquittal entirely, misrepresenting the hung jury on the lesser charge as she listed only 9-3 and did not mention the 12-0 vote on the primary charge, later telling the defense attorney that it was 9-3 on both charges. The defense had submitted a written record that preserved the truth. It can be read even though it was marked through. Cognitive Rationalizations in Misconduct Law enforcement officers and prosecutors often rely on cognitive rationalizations that sanitize misconduct and recast deviant conduct as necessary, harmless, or justified. Those rationalizations can operate before misconduct, by preempting guilt, and after misconduct, by neutralizing regret. Over time, they reshape an institution’s moral boundaries. Denial of Victim: The target is framed as deserving mistreatment. In a criminal case, that often appears as the view that a defendant is unworthy of fair treatment, full disclosure, or procedural protection. Denial of Responsibility: Misconduct is recast as unavoidable. Officers attribute it to pressure, culture, or necessity; prosecutors attribute it to caseload, politics, or the perceived need to “make the case stick.” Denial of Injury: The actor insists no real harm occurred. That mindset often appears when people dismiss suppressed evidence as immaterial or treat misleading testimony as inconsequential. Social Weighting: Misconduct is minimized by comparison to worse scandals elsewhere. That rhetorical move makes serious violations appear ordinary or trivial. Moral Justification: Rule-breaking is framed as necessary to accomplish a higher good. This is the most dangerous rationalization because it does not merely excuse misconduct; it portrays it as virtuous. Institutional Significance When these rationalizations become normalized, misconduct stops seeming exceptional and starts to seem righteous. In that environment, unlawful conduct is not merely tolerated. It is rewarded, repeated, and folded into institutional practice. Investigative Misconduct The misconduct in this case does not stem from a single mistake. They arise from recurring patterns: chronology drift, selective witness handling, evidentiary distortion, and testimonial evolution aligned with litigation needs. Investigative Undisclosed Familial Conflict Evidence: Major Freeman was Carmen Love’s brother-in-law. Carmen Love was Lauren Deal’s cousin. Freeman did not disclose this relationship to the court, the defense, or the magistrate. Love was not a neutral background witness — she was related by blood to the accuser and by marriage to the lead investigator. A third party later attempted to extort $150,000 from Allen to “drop the charges.” Freeman was informed and never followed up. Legal Standard Violated: IACP Code of Ethics (12 NCAC 10B.1102); due process; 12 NCAC 10B.0204(c); 10B.0301(12) Brother-in-Law Conflict of Interest Extortion Ignored Investigative Suppression or Distortion of Exculpatory Material Evidence: Freeman’s sworn affidavit attributed facts to Carmen Love’s recorded call that the recording plainly contradicts on every material point — including whether Love knew Allen, whether she saw Deal leave with him, and whether she had been trying to reach Deal all day. Affidavit claims “Mrs. Love stated that she saw Lauren… Lauren declined and stated she was going to go hang out with the guys and go to a bon fire. Mrs. Love told her to call her later… Mrs. Love stated that she became worried because she had been attempting to contact her all day.” What the recording actually says “When I went to leave, um, I asked Lauren to come with us… She said, ‘No. I’m gonna stay here.’ I said, ‘Okay.’ So I sent her the address, and we left.” “I haven’t spoken to her since.” On Ben Allen’s name: “Unmmmm — Ben Allen?… Nope. Doesn’t ring a bell.” Steve Happel’s interview — never referenced in the affidavit — described Deal as appearing unexpectedly and heavily intoxicated: “that girl kind of came out of nowhere… she gave someone her keys ‘cuz she was too drunk.” Legal Standard Violated: Brady v. Maryland ; Kyles v. Whitley ; Napue v. Illinois ; 12 NCAC 10B.0204(c) Brady Narrative Drift Affidavit Distortion Investigative Failure to Interview Material Witnesses Evidence: James Morrison and Peter West were both present at the bar that evening, yet neither was interviewed. Officer Haines’s initial report mentions neither name, underscoring that the investigation relied on narrative-supporting contacts and made no effort to locate those whose accounts could have confirmed or contradicted the timeline, social interactions, and intoxication narrative. Officer Haines report (verbatim) “SHE WENT TO SCHOOLY’S BAR WITH HER COUSIN CARMEN LOVE, AND WHILE THERE, MET BEN ALLEN, AND HIS FRIENDS JOSEPH DEMARCO AND A SUBJECT WITH THE FIRST NAME OF STEVE. SHE STATED THEY ALL DRANK TOGETHER, UNTIL 02:00 HRS, WITH CARMEN LOVE LEAVING THE BAR AT SOME POINT PRIOR DURING THE NIGHT.” Neither James Morrison nor Peter West appears anywhere in the Haines report. Their presence and observations were entirely absent from the investigative record. Legal Standard Violated: Basic investigative duty; due process concerns where omitted witnesses bear on credibility and probable cause Investigative Failure Material Witnesses Haines Report Investigative Probable Cause / Assignment Chronology Defect Evidence: The chronology in the testimony indicates that Detective Freeman became involved before the factual predicate was fully developed. Haines’s role was described as preliminary fact-gathering, yet Freeman’s timeline suggests the matter had already been escalated before that work was completed. Legal Standard Violated: Franks v. Delaware concerns where chronology and sworn representations materially diverge Franks Timeline Defect Investigative False or Impossible Report Timeline Evidence: Freeman’s account places case escalation before the interview chronology appears capable of supporting it. The sequence Haines and Freeman describe creates a structural timing problem that raises questions about when and how they fixed the case theory. Legal Standard Violated: Franks v. Delaware ; due process Franks Chronology Impossibility Investigative Destruction-of-Evidence Innuendo Without Foundation Evidence: The investigator later suggested that the cleanup behavior was consistent with destroying evidence, even though he had not processed the scene in a way that could establish whether evidence existed, where it existed, or whether anything had been removed. The insinuation extended to activity in a different room than the one where the assault was alleged to have occurred. Legal Standard Violated: Due process norms requiring factual foundation before prejudicial insinuation; fair-investigation principles Innuendo No Foundation Investigative Undocumented Probable Cause Presentation Evidence: Freeman orally presented probable cause to the magistrate and kept no contemporaneous notes or word-for-word record of what he said. Only one of the five sources he named had alleged an actual crime. The decisive “turning point” for arrest was not a newly discovered fact — it was the oral presentation itself, which cannot be audited or tested against Franks . Cruz: “I want to know what you presented.” Freeman: “Testimony to the magistrate. I mean, I don’t have word‑for‑word of what I presented to her.” Cruz: “It’s not in any of your notes or anything?” Freeman: “It’s not.” Cruz: “Through all those people you just named, only one of those persons had alleged an actual crime, correct?” Freeman: “Yes.” Legal Standard Violated: Franks v. Delaware , 438 U.S. 154 (1978); 12 NCAC 10B.0204(c); due process Franks No Notes Oral Presentation Investigative Custodial Status Misrepresentation Evidence: Freeman testified he had not decided to arrest Allen during the interview, yet left Allen guarded by another officer while he traveled to the magistrate. The magistrate’s order reflects a warrantless arrest; Freeman’s testimony blurs the legal moment when liberty was restrained and when Miranda obligations attached. He could not identify who was guarding Allen or on what authority the detention continued. Cruz: “Did you know you were going to arrest him at that point?” Freeman: “No, I did not.” Cruz: “Was that other officer standing outside the door?” Freeman: “Yes.” Legal Standard Violated: 4th Amendment; Miranda; 12 NCAC 10B.0204(c); LCSO Policy 02-13 Custodial Status Miranda 4th Amendment Investigative Suspect Rights Defects: DNA Consent & Right to Counsel Evidence: Freeman read only the first sentence of the DNA consent form, omitting the refusal-rights language in the second sentence. He never used the word “choice,” never told Allen he was free to leave, never advised Allen he could refuse to speak, and never informed him he had a right to an attorney. Allen had already asked about an attorney before being brought in. Cruz: “Did you read it in its entirety or just part of it?” Freeman: “No, I didn’t read it in the entirety…” Cruz: “You only stopped reading after the first sentence?” Freeman: “Well, yeah…” The sentence he skipped: “I have been informed by Detective Freeman that… I have a right to refuse to take my DNA.” Cruz: “Did you tell him that you have a choice to not do it?” Freeman: “I didn’t say it in those specific words, no, sir. Not ‘choice.’” Cruz: “Did you ever tell him that you don’t have to speak with me if you don’t want to?” Freeman: “Not that I recall.” Cruz: “Did you ever tell him… you do have a right to have an attorney here with you?” Freeman: “No, I didn’t.” Cruz: “He asked about [an attorney] earlier prior to coming down there, correct?” Freeman: “Yeah, he said, do I need an attorney?” Legal Standard Violated: 4th, 5th & 6th Amendments; Miranda; 12 NCAC 10B.0204(c); 10B.0301(12) DNA Consent Right to Counsel Miranda Investigative Principal Scene Never Processed Evidence: The bedroom alleged to be the scene of the assault was never forensically processed. Freeman took no photographs, measurements, or fingerprints; conducted no alternate-light-source examination; and collected no biological evidence from the bedding. Items recovered from the porch were collected without gloves or sealed packaging. The black pants seized under warrant were not promptly submitted for DNA analysis. A destruction-of-evidence insinuation was later advanced despite no baseline assessment of what had ever existed at the scene. Legal Standard Violated: BLET Manual (12 NCAC 10B.0502); LCSO Policy 07-07; 12 NCAC 10B.0301(12); 10B.1102 Scene Failure Chain of Custody Evidence Integrity Investigative Credential Discrepancy Under Oath Evidence: Freeman testified under oath that he held two advanced law-enforcement certificates — one through Criminal Justice Training Standards and one through Sheriffs’ Training Standards. The publicly available ACADIS certification record reflects neither certificate. If the certificates do not exist, Freeman’s sworn credential testimony raises an independent truthfulness issue under the Commission’s authority, separate from all other allegations. Legal Standard Violated: 12 NCAC 10B.0204(c)(1); G.S. 14-209 (perjury, if knowing); 10B.0301(12); 10B.1102 Credential Claim ACADIS Discrepancy Truthfulness Investigative 2:00 AM Bar Timeline: Video Proves Impossibility Evidence: The affidavit describes a 2:00 a.m. group conversation at the bar, where Deal agreed to attend the bonfire and told Carmen Love she was leaving. Bar surveillance video proves this is impossible: Carmen Love is seen exiting with James Morrison at 12:41:25 a.m. — before Deal had approached or spoken to anyone in the defendant’s group. Peter West left even earlier. The video shows no interaction between the groups while Love is present. The 2:00 a.m. departure narrative has no witness support and is directly contradicted by objective footage. Affidavit claim “They were at Schooly’s for several hours and at 2am Mrs. Deal stated she was asked by Ben and his friends if she wanted to go with them to Ben’s house and have a bon fire. She agreed and told Carmen Love that she was leaving with Ben and his friends.” Video record / Carmen Love (recorded call) Camera timestamp: Carmen Love exits at 12:41:25 a.m. with James Morrison — no interaction between groups is visible while Love is present. Love: “When I went to leave… She said, ‘No. I’m gonna stay here.’ I said, ‘Okay.’ So I sent her the address, and we left.” Carmen Love’s recorded call also names “Joseph” (DeMarco) despite having left the bar before Deal ever met him — indicating information was shared between them before Love’s police interview, which itself contradicts any claim of an independent account. Legal Standard Violated: Franks v. Delaware ; Napue v. Illinois ; 12 NCAC 10B.0204(c) Video Evidence 12:41 AM Exit Timeline Impossibility Investigative Affidavit Fabrication: “Ben Followed Her Inside” Evidence: The affidavit states the defendant “walked inside the house behind Lauren.” Not one witness said this. Both independent witnesses describe the two going inside together; neither describes the defendant following or pursuing Deal. The affidavit introduced the word “behind” — implying pursuit — where no witness used or implied that framing. Why would an investigator write such predatory framing into the file unless it was intentional? Affidavit “Upon getting to the house they started to build a fire and he walked inside the house behind Lauren while she went to the bathroom.” DeMarco (recorded) “We were collecting firewood, getting a fire going again. Lauren and Ben then went inside.” Happel (recorded) “I saw them go inside cuz she needed to use the bathroom.” Legal Standard Violated: Franks v. Delaware ; 12 NCAC 10B.0204(c); due process Franks Narrative Addition Witness Contradiction Investigative Affidavit Fabrication: DeMarco Did Not Search for Deal Evidence: The affidavit states DeMarco “made the decision to get his vehicle and ride in an attempt to locate her.” DeMarco’s own recorded statement says otherwise. He got afraid and left — he did not decide to search. He incidentally saw Deal while driving. Freeman upgraded a chance encounter into a deliberate search — a material change that shapes how Deal was found and implies active corroboration of her escape account. Additionally, Deal told police she was hiding behind a tree; DeMarco says he saw her running through a field. These accounts cannot both be true. Affidavit “Mr. DeMarco made the decision to get his vehicle and ride in an attempt to locate her and did so on the roadway, which was later identified as Old US 1.” DeMarco (recorded) “I was like… I woke up, I was just about to call the police, and then I get afraid and leave. Then, when I leave, I’m driving down the road near Route 1, and I see her running through a field.” Legal Standard Violated: Franks v. Delaware ; 12 NCAC 10B.0204(c); due process Franks DeMarco Account Material Substitution Physical Plausibility Analysis Major Freeman effected a felony arrest without inspecting the alleged scene or testing any physical premise of the accuser’s account against objective data. The account requires mutually incompatible conditions to coexist simultaneously — conditions the investigation never attempted to resolve. Lunar & Weather Conditions At 2:51 a.m. on October 19, 2019, the moon was approximately 75% illuminated (public lunar data). The temperature was 43°F at 93% humidity (NOAA records). The accuser claimed “complete darkness” and that conditions “felt good.” Neither claim matches the objective record. Freeman obtained neither dataset before the arrest. Terrain vs. Claimed Escape Route The direction the accuser described fleeing leads into an open, flat airfield — not woods and briars. To reach Route 1 as claimed, she would have had to reverse direction and run back toward the house. Freeman never walked the route, photographed it, or asked the accuser to explain the geographic impossibility. Witness Condition at the Bar Steve Happel’s uncontradicted trial testimony: “that girl kind of came out of nowhere and started being around us and acting kind of hysterical… she gave someone her keys ‘cuz she was too drunk…” This was never reconciled with the prosecution’s account of that evening. Irreconcilable Physics The testimony simultaneously requires: complete darkness; concealment in woods and briars; clear identification of a specific vehicle type; identification of the specific driver; mutual eye contact; and the driver waving from the highway. If darkness and concealment hold, identification collapses. If identification holds, darkness and concealment evaporate. These are not minor discrepancies — they are the central mechanics of the account. Physiological Constraints Never Evaluated The accuser’s reported height, weight, intoxication level, and footwear were never evaluated against the claimed ability to outrun two trained Army soldiers across rough terrain. The bed height (~36 in.), one-handed wrist-restraint mechanics, and simultaneous removal of tight clothing were never tested against basic biomechanics. What Was Never Done Photographs were taken at the scene — and that is where the investigation stopped. No measurements. No sketches. No route walk-through. No lunar or weather data obtained. No biomechanical assessment. They advanced the destruction-of-evidence insinuation without any baseline assessment of what evidence had ever existed at the scene. Prosecutorial Misconduct Prosecutorial Witness Coaching / Testimonial Tailoring Evidence: Lauren Deal’s speech patterns and substantive framing changed materially between her law-enforcement interviews and trial testimony. Those changes align with testimony that the prosecutor suggested narrative revisions tied to witness fear. Legal Standard Violated: Napue v. Illinois ; due process Napue Witness Coaching Prosecutorial Evidence Authentication Failure Evidence: Facebook messages identified as Exhibit 4 were presented without device metadata, custodial proof, or other foundational evidence sufficient to resolve the exhibit’s attribution problem, particularly where later screenshots identified another user of the phone. Legal Standard Violated: N.C. R. Evid. 901(a); Rule 104(b) Authentication Foundation Failure Prosecutorial Violation of Conditional Admission Limits Evidence: The court indicated Exhibit 4 was admissible only if the State linked it to the prior conversation to provide context. That foundational condition was not meaningfully satisfied, yet the State proceeded as though the condition had been met. Legal Standard Violated: N.C. R. Evid. 104(b); due process fairness concerns Rule 104(b) Conditional Admission Prosecutorial Rule of Completeness Violation Evidence: Only the first screenshot of the Facebook exchange was emphasized, while additional screenshots identifying another phone user were excluded from the State’s presentation, creating a misleading impression of authorship and continuity. Legal Standard Violated: N.C. R. Evid. 106 Rule 106 Misleading Sequence Prosecutorial Aggravating-Factor Manufacturing Evidence: The “position of trust” theory hardened only after testimony and framing evolved well beyond the initial statements and objective video context. The record supports an inference that the aggravator was constructed rather than organically supported. Legal Standard Violated: Due process; Brady ; Napue Aggravator Narrative Construction Prosecutorial Retaliatory Charging Pressure Evidence: Aggravating exposure increased after plea refusal, supporting the inference that charging leverage was used coercively rather than neutrally. Legal Standard Violated: Due process; prosecutorial ethics Retaliation Coercion Prosecutorial Misrepresentation of Forensic Evidence Evidence: The State’s presentation of forensic evidence materially affected defense strategy and was framed in a manner the defense contends was inaccurate, incomplete, or misleading. Legal Standard Violated: Brady ; due process; professional ethics Forensic Misconduct Prejudice Prosecutorial Shifting Injury Claims: Three Incompatible Accounts Evidence: Deal’s injury account evolved materially across three stages. The State presented each version without accounting for the prior contradictions. Freeman corrected his own in-court testimony after a lunch recess — changing where and when he observed injuries — suggesting the matter had been addressed during the break. Stage 1 — Deal to Officer Haines (recorded interview) “I have bruises on my arms from being held down. They took pictures of them at the hospital. They took a lot of pictures at the hospital.” Stage 2 — Freeman corrects his own testimony after recess Cruz: “I didn’t see that in the video. Was that in the video?” Freeman: “When she got there.” Cruz: “So prior to the interview?” Freeman: “Yeah, as we were going back.” [After lunch, Freeman returns to the stand and reverses this answer.] Cruz: “So this happened after the interview?” Freeman: “Yes.” Stage 3 — Deal at trial “Maybe a bruise on the front of her arm from when she got pushed down… that bruise may have come from falling in the woods.” No wrist bruises claimed. No hospital photographs referenced. No such photographs exist. On cross-examination, Haines confirmed Deal had told him the bruises were from being “held down” around the wrist — a claim Deal abandoned entirely at trial. Freeman continued to assert wrist injuries even after Deal had retracted that account. Legal Standard Violated: Napue v. Illinois ; Giglio v. United States ; duty not to present testimony the State knows to be inconsistent with the evidence Napue / Giglio Injury Contradiction Corrected Testimony Prosecutorial Facebook Exhibit: Judge’s Foundation Requirement Not Satisfied Evidence: State’s Exhibit 4 — a December 3, 2016 Facebook message — was conditionally admitted over defense objection. Defense counsel noted the exhibit’s own pages identify the sender as “Matt” using the defendant’s phone, and that the defendant himself states at the end that he did not have possession of his phone. The court admitted only the first page, conditioned on the State supplying testimony of a prior conversation before 1:49 p.m. that day. The State never elicited that testimony. Wunsch objection (trial record) “In this message, it clearly states — I mean, she is picking out part of it, but in this message, it clearly states that this is not Ben. It’s Matt. I’m using his phone… at the very end, Ben comes on, identified himself, saying, I didn’t have my phone. I’m sorry.” The Court’s condition for admission “If she testifies that they had a discussion prior to December 3, 2016, at 1:49, then that would give this particular page context… they will need to link this up with a conversation prior to December 3, 2016.” Bartholomew did not ask Deal whether she and the defendant had discussed the bonfire before 1:49 p.m. Having Deal read a text that says “Remember when I said I was having that bonfire…” is not independent testimony that the prior conversation occurred. The exhibit was introduced to support an aggravating factor — special position of trust — founded on a three-year-old partial screenshot in which the identified sender is disputed by the exhibit’s own content. Legal Standard Violated: N.C. R. Evid. 901; R. Evid. 106 (rule of completeness); due process; conditional admission obligations Authentication Failure Rule 901 / 106 Aggravating Factor Investigative & Prosecutorial Misconduct Framework Investigation Investigative Phase Failures Confirmation Bias: The case appears to have been escalated before the factual predicate was fully developed, suggesting a theory-first rather than evidence-first investigation. Selective Witnessing: Narrative-supporting witnesses were prioritized, while potentially exculpatory witnesses were not meaningfully pursued. Conflict of Interest: Familial and relational ties created, at a minimum, an appearance of compromised neutrality. Chronology Instability: Key reports and testimony do not align cleanly on when the detective became involved or how probable cause was formed. Bias Suppression Timeline Prosecution Prosecutorial Strategy Patterns Narrative Reconstruction: Trial testimony evolved in ways that cured weaknesses in the original account. Aggravator Expansion: Social familiarity was reframed into a more legally useful “position of trust” theory. Evidence Framing: The State relied on exhibits and theories that were presented more forcefully than they were grounded. Pressure Tactics: Increased exposure after plea refusal supports an inference of coercive leverage. Strategic Omission: Inconsistent or weakening material was not treated with the candor required of a minister of justice. Strategy Fabrication Omission Testimony Testimonial Fabrication Indicators Progressive Elaboration: Details multiplied over time, mapping neatly onto legal elements. Linguistic Shift: Content words changed more than function words, suggesting retraining rather than organic memory continuity. Retroactive Insertion: Themes such as fear, trust, freezing, and witness-related terror emerged more strongly at trial than in earlier accounts. Contradiction Cascade: Later details created tension with video, chronology, physical plausibility, and witness interviews. Disregard of Objective Video Evidence: Testimony proceeded as though surveillance video would not materially challenge the narrative. Fabrication Credibility Coaching Judicial Judicial Oversight Failures Authentication Relaxed: Evidence was allowed in despite unresolved foundation problems. Conditional Limits Not Enforced: The State proceeded beyond the court’s own qualification regarding admissibility. Lack of Enforcement: No meaningful corrective response appears to have followed despite repeated reliability concerns. Judicial Oversight Evidentiary Failure Constitutional Violations Constitutional 4th Amendment Violation: Arrest and detention without a properly grounded probable-cause foundation Impact: Unlawful seizure concerns; possible fruit-of-the-poisonous-tree consequences 4th Amendment Unlawful Arrest Constitutional 5th Amendment Violation: Vindictive or retaliatory charging pressure after plea refusal Impact: Coercive plea posture; increased exposure used as leverage 5th Amendment Vindictiveness Constitutional 6th Amendment - Effective Defense Violation: Misleading evidence presentation and late-shifting theories impaired the defense’s ability to prepare and respond Impact: Reduced ability to mount a complete and effective defense 6th Amendment Effective Defense Constitutional Due Process (14th Amendment) Violation: Suppression or distortion of exculpatory material, coached testimony, conflict-tainted investigation, and misleading evidentiary framing Impact: Fair-trial reliability substantially undermined 14th Amendment Due Process Constitutional Right to Confront Witnesses (6th Amendment) Violation: Narrative evolution and coaching concerns impaired meaningful cross-examination of credibility-critical witnesses Impact: The jury heard testimony whose evolution could not be fairly tested in real time 6th Amendment Confrontation Constitutional Right to Present Defense Violation: Material witnesses were not interviewed, exculpatory inconsistencies were not preserved with candor, and the defense was forced to answer shifting theories Impact: Incomplete factual record before the jury Defense Rights Suppression Constitutional Freedom from False or Misleading Evidence Violation: Improperly framed exhibits, unstable chronology, and testimony presented more definitively than the underlying record supports Impact: Verdict reliability compromised by a misleading factual foundation False Evidence Fabrication

records.text: Edifice of Lies Project Map Evidence Viewer Case Record Timeline Players Scene Analysis Evidence Documents Analysis Contradictions 40 Impeachment Cards Deal's Ever Changing Testimony New Face General Videos Inspired Digital Media Case Study Data Snapshot Diagrams Connections False Story Mindmaps Accountability Misconduct Prosecutor Conduct Judicial Duty System Essay Search Soundtrack A Statement of Indictment The New Face of Injustice “You can fool all the people some of the time, and some of the people all the time, but you cannot fool all the people all the time.” — Abraham Lincoln An forensic indictment of narrative construction, witness fabrication, and the institutional apparatus that shields prosecutorial and investigative misconduct in Lee County, North Carolina. On this page ➜ The Primary Figures ➜ Lady Justice of Lee County ➜ Narrative Engineering ➜ Investigative Complicity ➜ The Durham Lesson ➜ The Crumbling Foundation Tiffany Bartholomew Prosecutor • Narrative Architect Assistant District Attorney Responsible for transforming contradictory witness disclosures into polished trial testimony, introducing fabricated "position of trust" aggravating elements, and substituting emotional theater whenever physical evidence failed to support the State's theory. Coached key witnesses in courthouse hallways and during joint unrecorded prep sessions. Engineered narrative shifts from active physical struggle to traumatic freezing after forensics disproved force. Suborned testimony contradicted by contemporaneous 911 audio and CAD dispatches. Steve Freeman Lead Detective • Field Operative Sheriff's Office Conducting investigative inquiries with undisclosed family ties to primary witness Carmen Love, failing to secure physical crime scenes, altering witness interview summaries, and falsely claiming under oath that an arrest warrant existed when magistrate orders proved otherwise. Undisclosed familial relationship with witness Carmen Love during recorded interviews. Refused to secure or process the alleged scene, attending personal events instead. Sworn perjury regarding arrest warrant issuance, refuted by official court records. Iconographic Forensic Analysis Lady Justice of Lee County A forensic deconstruction of the altered symbols of justice: when scales of evidence are replaced by dual swords of unilateral force. 🔍 Click image to view full resolution exhibit Judgment Without Balance Traditionally, Lady Justice carries scales to signify deliberation, proportionality, and the weighing of evidence. The absence of scales removes evidentiary restraint. There is no weighing, no calibration, no pause. Two swords signify decisions rendered without proportional assessment—outcomes driven by assertion and institutional confidence rather than proof. Force Becomes Self-Reinforcing One sword represents authority constrained by constitutional law. Two swords represent authority reinforcing itself: enforcement stacked upon enforcement, power justified by its own momentum rather than legal legitimacy. Neutrality Abandoned The scales signify impartiality. Their absence, paired with dual weapons, transforms justice from an arbiter into an active combatant. The posture is adversarial. Justice is no longer an umpire—it has chosen a side, especially when the family of law enforcement is directly entangled. Institutional Self-Authorship The book beneath her is no longer revered; it is altered. We the People is crossed out. In its place stands an institutional name, implying authority without consent. The foundational charter is overwritten: authority no longer flows upward from the governed, but circulates internally as its own warrant. Restraint Rejected The blindfold remains, but its meaning is inverted. It no longer symbolizes impartiality; it symbolizes deliberate indifference. The system does not fail to see—it chooses not to look. The torn flag confirms the toll: legitimacy frayed, symbols retained only as an institutional backdrop. “Scales ask. Swords enforce. This image depicts a justice system that believes it no longer needs permission.” Part I • The Mechanics of Fabrication If Mike Nifong became the national symbol of a prosecutor who betrayed justice to preserve a false narrative, then Tiffany Bartholomew must become the symbol of something far more insidious: a prosecutor who did not merely protect a lie — she helped build it, shape it, coach it, polish it, and arm it for battle in open court. “When the facts failed, the questions changed. When the truth became inconvenient, emotion was substituted. When the evidence refused to carry the State where it wanted to go, pressure, coaching, and outright manipulation filled the void.” That is not prosecution. That is narrative engineering. That is not witness preparation. That is witness construction. Bartholomew did not merely ready the accuser for the stand — she rewrote the accuser's entire vocabulary, transforming raw accusation into courtroom-ready testimony. She crossed every line: switching from fact-based inquiry to emotional theater the moment manufactured evidence and coached lies could no longer bridge the gap. She intimidated witnesses in the courthouse and on joint calls with her detective. She had no boundary she wouldn't breach. “This is not preparation. This is fabrication with the full authority of the State behind it.” Part II • Investigative Complicity Detective Steve Freeman? He is the ideal partner for this operation: facts are suggestions, procedure is an obstacle, and accountability is strictly for defendants, never for the State. No urgency to secure the scene: Left the reported scene completely unsealed and unprocessed. No urgency to preserve evidence: Failed to collect timely physical evidence or inspect anatomical markers. No urgency to test the story against physical reality: Ignored forensic timelines that made the claimed narrative physically impossible. No concern for contradictions or conflicts of interest: Actively concealed direct familial connections to primary witnesses. He attended a family wedding instead of investigating. Crime-scene diagrams? Beneath him. Securing the reported crime scene? Immediate collection of physical evidence? That is for normal detectives. Freeman doesn't collect evidence — he manufactures it. He altered witness statements in his official reports — even though the original audio recordings went straight to the defense. On the stand, he lied about the arrest process, claiming an arrest warrant existed when the magistrate’s order — which everyone had a copy of — proved the opposite. “He did it because he knew, with absolute certainty, that nothing would happen. Nothing ever does.” Bartholomew was there to cover for him. She crafts the falsehoods; he delivers them. Subornation of perjury is not a scandal to her — it is a tool. Her only problem would be if her witnesses lacked the stomach to perjure themselves for a conviction. Part III • The Durham Lesson Inverted “This is what makes Bartholomew and Freeman more dangerous than Nifong ever was. Nifong became a scandal. His name became a stain. The system at least pretended to be shocked.” But these two — and the institution that shields them — have learned the real lesson from Durham: next time, be smarter about hiding it. Coach more carefully. Shade the facts more confidently. Close ranks faster. They acted with the calm assurance that the lines no longer mattered — because the system had already decided to protect its own once it committed to a false story. The defendant complained to counsel. Letters went to the State Bar. The record laid bare the contradictions. The machinery never slowed. “That is the public scandal here: not merely that falsehood was advanced, but that the entire apparatus of justice appeared willing to absorb it, defend it, and carry it forward as though truth were irrelevant.” Nifong’s disgrace at least became visible. Bartholomew and Freeman represent the next, more corrosive stage — when betrayal of justice is no longer reckless but disciplined; no longer shocking but routine; no longer hidden because it cannot be seen, but because the institutions that see it refuse to act. Mike Nifong should have been a warning that misconduct would not be tolerated. Instead, the 12th Prosecutorial District used his story as a training manual. Part IV • The Threat to Every Citizen This is not a procedural footnote. This is not an academic debate for law reviews. Because when prosecutors become storytellers and investigators become stagehands — when the machinery of justice exists only to control the narrative rather than discover the truth — then every citizen becomes a potential target of extortion by those who wear badges or carry the State’s seal. The system's legitimacy does not rest on the mythical perfection of its actors. It rests on their demonstrated willingness to police their own. When that willingness dies, the foundation does not merely crack. It crumbles. We are watching it crumble in real time. Truth still matters. Process still protects. Power must still answer to principle. Or we no longer have a justice system — we have a story factory with uniforms and gavels. And in Lee County, North Carolina, the machines are running at full speed. ×

records.section: The people at the center of this case did not meet as strangers. Several relationships existed before the accusation was made, and those pre-existing connections shaped who was investigated , who was interviewed , and who was protected . They used a previous allegation that was investigated by experts and the court to turn opinion against the defendant while never giving him the opportunity to defend against it.
records.text: The people at the center of this case did not meet as strangers. Several relationships existed before the accusation was made, and those pre-existing connections shaped who was investigated , who was interviewed , and who was protected . They used a previous allegation that was investigated by experts and the court to turn opinion against the defendant while never giving him the opportunity to defend against it. Defendant Benjamin Allen Defendant A military veteran and father living in Lee County. He had no prior relationship with Lauren Deal beyond a brief social connection through his ex-wife. He was present at Schooly’s bar on the night in question. He lost employment, housing stability, access to family, and years of his life to a prosecution built on a record that consistently contradicted the charge. He refused the extortion attempt. He refused the ADA’s plea deal that came with a threat. This man is the real victim in this case. Innocent Accuser Lauren Deal Accuser The primary complainant. Her initial police statements materially diverged from her trial testimony and from other statements the Detective gathered that evening. Multiple claimed facts—running through pitch-black woods, hiding behind trees, fleeing through briars—are physically inconsistent with the documented terrain, the recorded lunar conditions (approximately 70% illumination), and the scene’s layout. Her testimony evolved in ways that followed prosecutorial framing rather than her earlier statements. She claimed a connection to Allen through his ex-wife. Her social circle includes Joel Kelly, whose daughter was her best friend. Joel Kelly sent the extortion messages ($150,000 demand to make the case “go away”). Fabrication For Money Investigator Detective Steve Freeman Lead Investigator Perjury & Fabrication — Altered witness statements in official documents, contradicting recorded conversations available to the defense and giving the impression of guilt while misleading the court. False Probable Cause — Recast Carmen Love's initial exculpatory statement into one supporting probable cause, directly contradicting witness LD's account. Undisclosed Conflict of Interest — Failed to disclose a familial relationship with Love, a key witness who accompanied Deal to the bar that night. Suppression of Evidence — Claimed not to know other witnesses despite existing relationships and failed to do any crime scene analysis. An officer whose career spans over 27 years, holds advanced law enforcement certifications, instructor at a local college teaching criminal investigations, and was an instructor on FORENSIC EVIDENCE. At the supposed crime scene, his exploitation was limited to taking pictures. Conflict of Interest Evidence Suppression Prosecutor ADA Tiffany Bartholomew Lead Prosecutor The Assistant District Attorney who prosecuted the case. Accused of witness coaching, misrepresenting evidence, violating judicial instructions on the conditional admission of evidence (N.C. R. Evid. 104(b)), withholding the balance of exhibits under the rule of completeness (N.C. R. Evid. 106), and constructing an unsupported “position of trust” aggravating factor. Deal’s speech register and substantive framing shifted materially between law-enforcement interviews and trial—changes that aligned with Bartholomew’s litigation strategy. Known for underhanded tactics and for receiving special treatment in Lee County courtrooms. Witness Coaching Evidence Fabrication Key Witness Carmen Love Key Witness / Freeman’s Relative Deal’s cousin. Present at the bar that night with Deal. Her initial recorded statement to Freeman—her relative—did not identify Allen by name and contradicted the narrative later advanced in the investigation. Freeman claimed to have used that interview to establish probable cause, despite its exculpatory content. Love’s later interviews matched or even exceeded the narrative engineering of the prosecution’s account. The two uninterviewed witnesses at the scene—James Morrison (Love’s boyfriend) and Peter West III (father works in the Lee County Sheriff’s Office)—were never called, which means every account from within that evening’s group was filtered through people with undisclosed connections to the investigator. Suppressed Evidence Initial Officer Officer Isaac Haines Initial Responding Officer Conducted the first interview with Lauren Deal. Testified his role was fact-finding to determine if the case warranted a detective assignment, creating a timeline contradiction since Freeman testified he had already been notified about a sexual assault allegation before the interview with Deal had even begun. Stated the role of himself and Freeman as: “to prove that he (Allen) is guilty.” Got promoted to Detective after this case. Witness Joseph DeMarco Eyewitness Present at Schooly’s bar and at Allen’s residence. Picked up Deal after the alleged incident. Fear and intimidation initially led him to lie about events, such as picking Deal up on the road. They both had different stories about that event. His later (missing) statement contradicts Deal’s trial narrative on multiple points. Witness Steven Happel Eyewitness Present at the bar and residence. Testimony provides an alternative timeline and contradicts Deal’s claims about physical contact and behavior. His testimony matches what is on video, unlike Deal’s. Third Party Joel Kelly Third Party with Financial Motive Sent the $150,000 extortion demand in text messages to Allen. Kelly’s daughter was one of Deal’s best friends. Another of Deal’s best friends, Pamella Kells, worked for Joel Kelly. He was embedded in the same social network as Deal and shared overlapping connections with individuals who had reason to fabricate or amplify the allegation. The extortion contact preceded the formal complaint, establishing a financial motive that the investigation did not adequately explore. Extortion Attempt Missing Witnesses James Morrison & Peter West Missing Witnesses Both were present at Schooly’s bar on the night in question. Neither was interviewed by investigators. Morrison was Carmen Love’s boyfriend, placing him in her direct social circle—and thus in Freeman’s undisclosed network. West’s father works at the Sheriff’s Office and signed Allen’s release from jail. Their unrecorded observations of Deal’s behavior, apparent intoxication, and movements that evening would have been directly material to the credibility of the complaint. Their absence from the investigative record is not explained. Witness Suppression Antagonist Jolynda Adcock Personal Antagonist Demonstrated long-standing personal animosity toward Allen. Sexually exploited Allen’s ex-wife’s documented mental illness. Stated explicitly that “it didn’t matter whether Mr. Allen was innocent” due to the Sheriff’s Department connections available to the complainant’s circle. That statement is one of the most direct documentary records in this archive of how those within the case understood the structural environment around it. The implausible and changing stories are explained in one line. Law Enforcement Manipulation

records.section: When the ADA Is More Powerful Than the DA And There Is No Judicial Standard
records.text: When the ADA Is More Powerful Than the DA And There Is No Judicial Standard Central Issue The State Had to Authenticate More Than a Screenshot State’s Exhibit 4 was offered as a Facebook Messenger communication authored by Ben Allen. That required proof of two separate propositions: first, that the screenshot accurately reflected what appeared on Lauren Deal’s phone; and second, that Ben actually authored the specific message attributed to him. Deal could identify what appeared on her own device. The harder question was authorship. The complete thread showed that another person, “Matt,” used Ben’s phone and identified himself within the same exchange. That fact did not conclusively prove Matt wrote the earlier message, but it defeated any assumption that the display name “Ben Allen” alone established who pressed send. The State authenticated the image only marginally, did not adequately establish the witness’s personal basis for attributing the disputed message to Ben, failed to satisfy the factual condition imposed by the court, and then obtained a judicial statement to the jury that the evidence was “sufficiently reliable.” What the Record Shows The Sequence Matters Deal identified the exhibit as messages on her phone and agreed, through leading questions, that they were messages “between” her and Ben. The defense objected that the State had selected only one page even though later pages stated that “Matt” was using Ben’s phone and that Ben later denied possessing it. The judge acknowledged the third-party-access problem and required the State to connect the first message to a specific earlier bonfire discussion. Bartholomew did not clearly establish when, how, or with whom that prior bonfire discussion occurred. The judge nevertheless told the jury that the exhibit was admissible and “sufficiently reliable.” When the exhibit was published, the judge further described it as corroborative without explaining its limited purpose or resolving the authorship problem. Testimony Concerning State’s Exhibit 4 MS. BARTHOLOMEW: Okay. And what social media platform was that? LAUREN DEAL: Facebook. MS. BARTHOLOMEW: And did you ever communicate with the defendant through Facebook? LAUREN DEAL: Yes. MS. BARTHOLOMEW: Your Honor, may I approach the witness? THE COURT: Yes. MS. BARTHOLOMEW: Lauren, I’m handing you what has been marked for identification purposes as State’s Exhibit Number 4. Do you recognize State’s Exhibit Number 4? LAUREN DEAL: Yes. MS. BARTHOLOMEW: What do you recognize State’s Exhibit Number 4 to be? LAUREN DEAL: Messages between me and Ben. MS. BARTHOLOMEW: When you were contacting him, or he was contacting you, through Facebook, how did that work? Was that on a laptop, a cell phone, or something else? LAUREN DEAL: For me? MS. BARTHOLOMEW: Yes. LAUREN DEAL: My cell phone. MS. BARTHOLOMEW: Were you able to retrieve any messages between yourself and Mr. Allen using Facebook? LAUREN DEAL: Facebook Messenger, yes. MS. BARTHOLOMEW: Facebook Messenger is an application that allows you to send direct messages to another person? LAUREN DEAL: Yes. MS. BARTHOLOMEW: State’s Exhibit Number 4 is the beginning of a conversation you had with the defendant in this matter, Mr. Allen? LAUREN DEAL: Yes. MS. BARTHOLOMEW: Do you know how the State came into possession of State’s Exhibit Number 4? LAUREN DEAL: I gave them to you. MS. BARTHOLOMEW: Do you still have the messages on your actual cell phone? LAUREN DEAL: Yes. MS. BARTHOLOMEW: Is State's Exhibit Number 4 an exact copy of the messages from 2016 between you and the defendant? LAUREN DEAL: Yes. MS. BARTHOLOMEW: Your Honor, at this time, the State would introduce State's Exhibit Number 4. MR. WUNSCH: Objection. THE COURT: What is the basis of your objection? MR. WUNSCH: In this message, it clearly states—mean, she is picking out part of it—but the message clearly states, "This is not Ben. It's Matt. I'm using his phone." The last message later states that Ben said, "I wasn't even—I didn't even have possession of my phone. Matt had my phone." So it is not Ben. It is clearly stated in the text that it is not Ben. We are picking out one page. THE COURT: What are you referring to? Actually, let me see the attorneys first. MR. WUNSCH: There is a— THE COURT: Just approach, please. [An off-the-record discussion was held at the bench.] THE COURT: All right. Ladies and gentlemen, I’ll ask you to go back into the jury room for just one moment while I sort this out. [The jury exited the courtroom.] Argument Outside the Presence of the Jury THE COURT: Let the record reflect that the jurors are now back in the jury room. The Court is reviewing what appears to be—I guess this is the seven—are there seven total? There are six on these sheets. MS. BARTHOLOMEW: Yes. Yes, Your Honor. THE COURT: Okay. What appears to be seven screenshots of purported messages. Anything further that the defense wants to say? MR. WUNSCH: It also lacks foundation, Your Honor. We just know that we have a screenshot of a Facebook message. My real problem, though, Your Honor, is that it identifies another person as conducting the conversation. At the very end, Ben comes on, identifies himself, and says, "I didn't have my phone. I'm sorry." So it is clearly not—we have someone else identifying himself. We do not have that person here. Therefore, Your Honor, we object to this page of Facebook screenshots being entered into evidence. THE COURT: All right. The Court has reviewed State's Exhibit Number 4. It is a screenshot that this witness indicated came from her phone. She has identified it. It says "Ben Allen" and contains the date December 3, 2016, at 1:49 p.m. It references a discussion they purportedly had about a bonfire. If she testifies that they had a discussion before December 3, 2016, at 1:49 p.m., that would give this particular page context. It is true that the remaining pages, beginning on page two, suggest that another individual was using his phone. However, that occurs later in the evening, at 7:42 p.m. There is no reason to believe that the first message was not from Ben Allen, particularly if it refers to an earlier conversation about a bonfire. If the defense wants some of the other pages admitted under the rule of completeness, I will allow that. Even the State concedes that those later messages appear to have been sent by another individual. The State is not attempting to introduce statements purportedly made by Matt while using Ben's phone. The State is simply attempting to introduce the first page. Again, the State will need to link this exhibit to a conversation that occurred before December 3, 2016. I believe you had that. I'll pass these back to the State. MR. WUNSCH: Your Honor, we would just note our objection for the record. THE COURT: All right. You can bring them back in. [The jury entered the courtroom and was seated in the jury box.] Court's Ruling THE COURT: Ladies and gentlemen, in my discretion, I have overruled the objection and found proposed State's Exhibit Number 4 to be admissible and sufficiently reliable to be admitted. Testimony Regarding the Contents of State's Exhibit 4 MS. BARTHOLOMEW: Lauren, is there a date associated with the messages in State's Exhibit Number 4? LAUREN DEAL: December 3, 2016. MS. BARTHOLOMEW: At what time does the first message appear? LAUREN DEAL: 1:49 p.m. MS. BARTHOLOMEW: Who sent the first message in State's Exhibit Number 4? LAUREN DEAL: Ben. MS. BARTHOLOMEW: What does it say? LAUREN DEAL: "Remember when I said I was having that bonfire on the 10th? It is tonight. Sorry for the short notice." MS. BARTHOLOMEW: Did you reply to that message? LAUREN DEAL: Yes, about three hours later. MS. BARTHOLOMEW: Is there a timestamp showing when your reply was made? LAUREN DEAL: 4:39. MS. BARTHOLOMEW: Did you reply? LAUREN DEAL: "I don't have a babysitter." MS. BARTHOLOMEW: Was there any conversation after that? LAUREN DEAL: He said, "Dang," then sent a picture of the bonfire. Then I said, "Yeah, I know." MS. BARTHOLOMEW: Your Honor, at this time, the State asks to publish State's Exhibit Number 4, the Facebook Messenger message, to the jury. THE COURT: All right. MR. WUNSCH: We renew our objection. THE COURT: All right. Again, the Court finds that this is for corroborative purposes. MR. WUNSCH: Noted for the record. Additional Testimony Concerning the Exhibit MS. BARTHOLOMEW: Lauren, we are looking at State's Exhibit Number 4. It may be slightly difficult to read the timestamps from where you are seated. Are you able to see them? LAUREN DEAL: No. MS. BARTHOLOMEW: If you moved closer, could you see the timestamps? LAUREN DEAL: Yes. MS. BARTHOLOMEW: State's Exhibit Number 4 reflects what you told the jury—that you communicated with the defendant through Facebook Messenger? LAUREN DEAL: Way prior to this, yes. MS. BARTHOLOMEW: What year did the conversation shown in State's Exhibit Number 4 take place? LAUREN DEAL: 2016. Rules 104(b), 901, and 602 Authentication Required Proof of Authorship, Not Merely Account Appearance Rule 901 requires evidence sufficient to support a finding that an exhibit is what its proponent claims. For electronic communications offered as a defendant’s own statements, authentication must address both the accuracy of the captured image and the identity of the author. Deal’s testimony that the screenshot came from her phone could authenticate the appearance of the screenshot. It did not automatically establish that Ben possessed his phone or authored the 1:49 p.m. message. Because the same thread showed another person using the device, the State needed additional circumstantial or direct evidence connecting Ben to that particular message. The critical foundation should have included the facts underlying Deal’s conclusion: whether she had previously discussed that exact bonfire with Ben, when and how that discussion occurred, whether the content contained information uniquely known to him, whether he later acknowledged the message, and how she knew who controlled the phone at 1:49 p.m. Rule 104(b) The judge conditioned admission on proof of a prior bonfire conversation. Conditional relevance permits temporary admission only if the promised foundation is later supplied. If it is not supplied, the evidence should be excluded or stricken. Rule 901(a) A display name and a screenshot from the recipient’s phone are not necessarily enough when the record affirmatively shows third-party access to the sender’s device or account. Rule 602 The witness needed a factual basis for knowing who authored the message. A bare answer that “Ben” sent it states the conclusion without establishing personal knowledge of device possession or authorship. The Unmet Condition Bartholomew Did Not Establish the Link the Judge Required The judge twice stated that the State needed to link the screenshot to a conversation occurring before 1:49 p.m. on December 3, 2016. That condition was not advisory. It was the court’s stated basis for treating the bonfire reference as circumstantial evidence of authorship. After the jury returned, Bartholomew established the date, timestamp, displayed sender, content of the message, Deal’s reply, and a later photograph of the bonfire. She did not clearly ask Deal whether she had previously discussed that specific bonfire with Ben, when the conversation occurred, how it occurred, or how she knew the earlier conversation was with him. The later answer, “Way prior to this, yes,” concerned Facebook communication generally. It did not clearly establish the specific prior bonfire discussion the court identified as the necessary factual link. The State therefore substituted Deal’s conclusion—“Ben”—for the foundational facts the judge had required. The Strongest Judicial Error The Court Shifted the Burden and Then Vouched for the Exhibit “There is no reason to believe that the first message was not from Ben Allen.” That formulation inverted Rule 901. The defense did not bear the burden of proving that Ben did not send the message. The State, as proponent, had to introduce affirmative evidence sufficient to support a finding that he did. The correct question was whether the State produced a factual basis from which a reasonable juror could attribute the message to Ben—not whether the defense disproved authorship. “I have overruled the objection and found proposed State’s Exhibit Number 4 to be admissible and sufficiently reliable to be admitted.” The court could announce that the exhibit was admitted. It should not have told the jury that disputed evidence was “sufficiently reliable.” Reliability, authorship, credibility, and evidentiary weight were the contested factual questions. records.title: State v. Benjamin Allen — State's Exhibit 4
records.section: The State Had to Authenticate More Than a Screenshot
records.text: The State Had to Authenticate More Than a Screenshot State’s Exhibit 4 was offered as a Facebook Messenger communication authored by Ben Allen. That required proof of two separate propositions: first, that the screenshot accurately reflected what appeared on Lauren Deal’s phone; and second, that Ben actually authored the specific message attributed to him. Deal could identify what appeared on her own device. The harder question was authorship. The complete thread showed that another person, “Matt,” used Ben’s phone and identified himself within the same exchange. That fact did not conclusively prove Matt wrote the earlier message, but it defeated any assumption that the display name “Ben Allen” alone established who pressed send. The State authenticated the image only marginally, did not adequately establish the witness’s personal basis for attributing the disputed message to Ben, failed to satisfy the factual condition imposed by the court, and then obtained a judicial statement to the jury that the evidence was “sufficiently reliable.”

records.text: The Sequence Matters Deal identified the exhibit as messages on her phone and agreed, through leading questions, that they were messages “between” her and Ben. The defense objected that the State had selected only one page even though later pages stated that “Matt” was using Ben’s phone and that Ben later denied possessing it. The judge nevertheless told the jury that the exhibit was admissible and “sufficiently reliable.” When the exhibit was published, the judge further described it as corroborative without explaining its limited purpose or resolving the authorship problem.

records.section: Authentication Required Proof of Authorship, Not Merely Account Appearance
records.text: Authentication Required Proof of Authorship, Not Merely Account Appearance Rule 901 requires evidence sufficient to support a finding that an exhibit is what its proponent claims. For electronic communications offered as a defendant’s own statements, authentication must address both the accuracy of the captured image and the identity of the author. Deal’s testimony that the screenshot came from her phone could authenticate the appearance of the screenshot. It did not automatically establish that Ben possessed his phone or authored the 1:49 p.m. message. Because the same thread showed another person using the device, the State needed additional circumstantial or direct evidence connecting Ben to that particular message. The critical foundation should have included the facts underlying Deal’s conclusion: whether she had previously discussed that exact bonfire with Ben, when and how that discussion occurred, whether the content contained information uniquely known to him, whether he later acknowledged the message, and how she knew who controlled the phone at 1:49 p.m. Rule 104(b) The judge conditioned admission on proof of a prior bonfire conversation. Conditional relevance permits temporary admission only if the promised foundation is later supplied. If it is not supplied, the evidence should be excluded or stricken. Rule 901(a) A display name and a screenshot from the recipient’s phone are not necessarily enough when the record affirmatively shows third-party access to the sender’s device or account. Rule 602 The witness needed a factual basis for knowing who authored the message. A bare answer that “Ben” sent it states the conclusion without establishing personal knowledge of device possession or authorship.

records.section: Bartholomew Did Not Establish the Link the Judge Required
records.text: Bartholomew Did Not Establish the Link the Judge Required The judge twice stated that the State needed to link the screenshot to a conversation occurring before 1:49 p.m. on December 3, 2016. That condition was not advisory. It was the court’s stated basis for treating the bonfire reference as circumstantial evidence of authorship. After the jury returned, Bartholomew established the date, timestamp, displayed sender, content of the message, Deal’s reply, and a later photograph of the bonfire. She did not clearly ask Deal whether she had previously discussed that specific bonfire with Ben, when the conversation occurred, how it occurred, or how she knew the earlier conversation was with him. The later answer, “Way prior to this, yes,” concerned Facebook communication generally. It did not clearly establish the specific prior bonfire discussion the court identified as the necessary factual link. The State therefore substituted Deal’s conclusion—“Ben”—for the foundational facts the judge had required.

records.section: When The Prosecutor and the Judge Team Up
records.text: When The Prosecutor and the Judge Team Up The State did not simply offer a screenshot. It offered the screenshot as Ben Allen’s own statement. Yet the complete thread disclosed third-party access; the State did not clearly establish the specific prior conversation the judge required, and the witness was permitted to state the ultimate conclusion of authorship without explaining how she knew it. The judge then shifted the authentication burden by reasoning that there was no reason to believe Ben did not send the message. Most significantly, the judge told the jury that the exhibit was “sufficiently reliable,” placing judicial authority behind evidence whose authorship and weight remained disputed. The strongest preserved issue would have combined Rules 104(b), 901, 602, 106, and 403 at admission, followed by an immediate § 15A-1222 objection, request for a curative instruction, and—if the prejudice could not be cured—a motion for mistrial under § 15A-1061.
