records.section: State v. Benjamin Allen — State's Exhibit 4
records.text: Edifice of Lies Project Map Evidence Viewer Case Record Timeline Players Scene Analysis Evidence Documents Analysis Contradictions 40 Impeachment Cards Deal's Ever Changing Testimony New Face General Videos Inspired Digital Media Case Study Data Snapshot Diagrams Connections False Story Mindmaps Accountability Misconduct Prosecutor Conduct Judicial Duty System Essay Search Soundtrack State’s Exhibit 4 “Silence is never neutral; in the presence of wrongdoing, it becomes complicity.” On this page Overview Record Summary Exhibit 4 Testimony Authentication Judicial Error Strongest Objection Rules and Duties Bottom Line A Disputed Screenshot, an Unmet Foundation, and a Court That Told the Jury It Was “Reliable” When the ADA Is More Powerful Than the DA And There Is No Judicial Standard Central Issue The State Had to Authenticate More Than a Screenshot State’s Exhibit 4 was offered as a Facebook Messenger communication authored by Ben Allen. That required proof of two separate propositions: first, that the screenshot accurately reflected what appeared on Lauren Deal’s phone; and second, that Ben actually authored the specific message attributed to him. Deal could identify what appeared on her own device. The harder question was authorship. The complete thread showed that another person, “Matt,” used Ben’s phone and identified himself within the same exchange. That fact did not conclusively prove Matt wrote the earlier message, but it defeated any assumption that the display name “Ben Allen” alone established who pressed send. The State authenticated the image only marginally, did not adequately establish the witness’s personal basis for attributing the disputed message to Ben, failed to satisfy the factual condition imposed by the court, and then obtained a judicial statement to the jury that the evidence was “sufficiently reliable.” What the Record Shows The Sequence Matters Deal identified the exhibit as messages on her phone and agreed, through leading questions, that they were messages “between” her and Ben. The defense objected that the State had selected only one page even though later pages stated that “Matt” was using Ben’s phone and that Ben later denied possessing it. The judge acknowledged the third-party-access problem and required the State to connect the first message to a specific earlier bonfire discussion. Bartholomew did not clearly establish when, how, or with whom that prior bonfire discussion occurred. The judge nevertheless told the jury that the exhibit was admissible and “sufficiently reliable.” When the exhibit was published, the judge further described it as corroborative without explaining its limited purpose or resolving the authorship problem. Testimony Concerning State’s Exhibit 4 MS. BARTHOLOMEW: Okay. And what social media platform was that? LAUREN DEAL: Facebook. MS. BARTHOLOMEW: And did you ever communicate with the defendant through Facebook? LAUREN DEAL: Yes. MS. BARTHOLOMEW: Your Honor, may I approach the witness? THE COURT: Yes. MS. BARTHOLOMEW: Lauren, I’m handing you what has been marked for identification purposes as State’s Exhibit Number 4. Do you recognize State’s Exhibit Number 4? LAUREN DEAL: Yes. MS. BARTHOLOMEW: What do you recognize State’s Exhibit Number 4 to be? LAUREN DEAL: Messages between me and Ben. MS. BARTHOLOMEW: When you were contacting him, or he was contacting you, through Facebook, how did that work? Was that on a laptop, a cell phone, or something else? LAUREN DEAL: For me? MS. BARTHOLOMEW: Yes. LAUREN DEAL: My cell phone. MS. BARTHOLOMEW: Were you able to retrieve any messages between yourself and Mr. Allen using Facebook? LAUREN DEAL: Facebook Messenger, yes. MS. BARTHOLOMEW: Facebook Messenger is an application that allows you to send direct messages to another person? LAUREN DEAL: Yes. MS. BARTHOLOMEW: State’s Exhibit Number 4 is the beginning of a conversation you had with the defendant in this matter, Mr. Allen? LAUREN DEAL: Yes. MS. BARTHOLOMEW: Do you know how the State came into possession of State’s Exhibit Number 4? LAUREN DEAL: I gave them to you. MS. BARTHOLOMEW: Do you still have the messages on your actual cell phone? LAUREN DEAL: Yes. MS. BARTHOLOMEW: Is State's Exhibit Number 4 an exact copy of the messages from 2016 between you and the defendant? LAUREN DEAL: Yes. MS. BARTHOLOMEW: Your Honor, at this time, the State would introduce State's Exhibit Number 4. MR. WUNSCH: Objection. THE COURT: What is the basis of your objection? MR. WUNSCH: In this message, it clearly states—mean, she is picking out part of it—but the message clearly states, "This is not Ben. It's Matt. I'm using his phone." The last message later states that Ben said, "I wasn't even—I didn't even have possession of my phone. Matt had my phone." So it is not Ben. It is clearly stated in the text that it is not Ben. We are picking out one page. THE COURT: What are you referring to? Actually, let me see the attorneys first. MR. WUNSCH: There is a— THE COURT: Just approach, please. [An off-the-record discussion was held at the bench.] THE COURT: All right. Ladies and gentlemen, I’ll ask you to go back into the jury room for just one moment while I sort this out. [The jury exited the courtroom.] Argument Outside the Presence of the Jury THE COURT: Let the record reflect that the jurors are now back in the jury room. The Court is reviewing what appears to be—I guess this is the seven—are there seven total? There are six on these sheets. MS. BARTHOLOMEW: Yes. Yes, Your Honor. THE COURT: Okay. What appears to be seven screenshots of purported messages. Anything further that the defense wants to say? MR. WUNSCH: It also lacks foundation, Your Honor. We just know that we have a screenshot of a Facebook message. My real problem, though, Your Honor, is that it identifies another person as conducting the conversation. At the very end, Ben comes on, identifies himself, and says, "I didn't have my phone. I'm sorry." So it is clearly not—we have someone else identifying himself. We do not have that person here. Therefore, Your Honor, we object to this page of Facebook screenshots being entered into evidence. THE COURT: All right. The Court has reviewed State's Exhibit Number 4. It is a screenshot that this witness indicated came from her phone. She has identified it. It says "Ben Allen" and contains the date December 3, 2016, at 1:49 p.m. It references a discussion they purportedly had about a bonfire. If she testifies that they had a discussion before December 3, 2016, at 1:49 p.m., that would give this particular page context. It is true that the remaining pages, beginning on page two, suggest that another individual was using his phone. However, that occurs later in the evening, at 7:42 p.m. There is no reason to believe that the first message was not from Ben Allen, particularly if it refers to an earlier conversation about a bonfire. If the defense wants some of the other pages admitted under the rule of completeness, I will allow that. Even the State concedes that those later messages appear to have been sent by another individual. The State is not attempting to introduce statements purportedly made by Matt while using Ben's phone. The State is simply attempting to introduce the first page. Again, the State will need to link this exhibit to a conversation that occurred before December 3, 2016. I believe you had that. I'll pass these back to the State. MR. WUNSCH: Your Honor, we would just note our objection for the record. THE COURT: All right. You can bring them back in. [The jury entered the courtroom and was seated in the jury box.] Court's Ruling THE COURT: Ladies and gentlemen, in my discretion, I have overruled the objection and found proposed State's Exhibit Number 4 to be admissible and sufficiently reliable to be admitted. Testimony Regarding the Contents of State's Exhibit 4 MS. BARTHOLOMEW: Lauren, is there a date associated with the messages in State's Exhibit Number 4? LAUREN DEAL: December 3, 2016. MS. BARTHOLOMEW: At what time does the first message appear? LAUREN DEAL: 1:49 p.m. MS. BARTHOLOMEW: Who sent the first message in State's Exhibit Number 4? LAUREN DEAL: Ben. MS. BARTHOLOMEW: What does it say? LAUREN DEAL: "Remember when I said I was having that bonfire on the 10th? It is tonight. Sorry for the short notice." MS. BARTHOLOMEW: Did you reply to that message? LAUREN DEAL: Yes, about three hours later. MS. BARTHOLOMEW: Is there a timestamp showing when your reply was made? LAUREN DEAL: 4:39. MS. BARTHOLOMEW: Did you reply? LAUREN DEAL: "I don't have a babysitter." MS. BARTHOLOMEW: Was there any conversation after that? LAUREN DEAL: He said, "Dang," then sent a picture of the bonfire. Then I said, "Yeah, I know." MS. BARTHOLOMEW: Your Honor, at this time, the State asks to publish State's Exhibit Number 4, the Facebook Messenger message, to the jury. THE COURT: All right. MR. WUNSCH: We renew our objection. THE COURT: All right. Again, the Court finds that this is for corroborative purposes. MR. WUNSCH: Noted for the record. Additional Testimony Concerning the Exhibit MS. BARTHOLOMEW: Lauren, we are looking at State's Exhibit Number 4. It may be slightly difficult to read the timestamps from where you are seated. Are you able to see them? LAUREN DEAL: No. MS. BARTHOLOMEW: If you moved closer, could you see the timestamps? LAUREN DEAL: Yes. MS. BARTHOLOMEW: State's Exhibit Number 4 reflects what you told the jury—that you communicated with the defendant through Facebook Messenger? LAUREN DEAL: Way prior to this, yes. MS. BARTHOLOMEW: What year did the conversation shown in State's Exhibit Number 4 take place? LAUREN DEAL: 2016. Rules 104(b), 901, and 602 Authentication Required Proof of Authorship, Not Merely Account Appearance Rule 901 requires evidence sufficient to support a finding that an exhibit is what its proponent claims. For electronic communications offered as a defendant’s own statements, authentication must address both the accuracy of the captured image and the identity of the author. Deal’s testimony that the screenshot came from her phone could authenticate the appearance of the screenshot. It did not automatically establish that Ben possessed his phone or authored the 1:49 p.m. message. Because the same thread showed another person using the device, the State needed additional circumstantial or direct evidence connecting Ben to that particular message. The critical foundation should have included the facts underlying Deal’s conclusion: whether she had previously discussed that exact bonfire with Ben, when and how that discussion occurred, whether the content contained information uniquely known to him, whether he later acknowledged the message, and how she knew who controlled the phone at 1:49 p.m. Rule 104(b) The judge conditioned admission on proof of a prior bonfire conversation. Conditional relevance permits temporary admission only if the promised foundation is later supplied. If it is not supplied, the evidence should be excluded or stricken. Rule 901(a) A display name and a screenshot from the recipient’s phone are not necessarily enough when the record affirmatively shows third-party access to the sender’s device or account. Rule 602 The witness needed a factual basis for knowing who authored the message. A bare answer that “Ben” sent it states the conclusion without establishing personal knowledge of device possession or authorship. The Unmet Condition Bartholomew Did Not Establish the Link the Judge Required The judge twice stated that the State needed to link the screenshot to a conversation occurring before 1:49 p.m. on December 3, 2016. That condition was not advisory. It was the court’s stated basis for treating the bonfire reference as circumstantial evidence of authorship. After the jury returned, Bartholomew established the date, timestamp, displayed sender, content of the message, Deal’s reply, and a later photograph of the bonfire. She did not clearly ask Deal whether she had previously discussed that specific bonfire with Ben, when the conversation occurred, how it occurred, or how she knew the earlier conversation was with him. The later answer, “Way prior to this, yes,” concerned Facebook communication generally. It did not clearly establish the specific prior bonfire discussion the court identified as the necessary factual link. The State therefore substituted Deal’s conclusion—“Ben”—for the foundational facts the judge had required. The Strongest Judicial Error The Court Shifted the Burden and Then Vouched for the Exhibit “There is no reason to believe that the first message was not from Ben Allen.” That formulation inverted Rule 901. The defense did not bear the burden of proving that Ben did not send the message. The State, as proponent, had to introduce affirmative evidence sufficient to support a finding that he did. The correct question was whether the State produced a factual basis from which a reasonable juror could attribute the message to Ben—not whether the defense disproved authorship. “I have overruled the objection and found proposed State’s Exhibit Number 4 to be admissible and sufficiently reliable to be admitted.” The court could announce that the exhibit was admitted. It should not have told the jury that disputed evidence was “sufficiently reliable.” Reliability, authorship, credibility, and evidentiary weight were the contested factual questions. By using the court’s institutional authority to characterize the exhibit as reliable, the judge risked endorsing Deal’s attribution and the State’s theory in violation of N.C. Gen. Stat. § 15A-1222. The later statement that the exhibit was admitted “for corroborative purposes” compounded the problem. Corroboration cannot substitute for authentication. Nor can the exhibit independently corroborate the witness’s authorship conclusion until authorship has first been adequately established. Rule 106 and Rule 403 The State Presented the Page Most Favorable to Its Theory The defense alerted the court that the State was offering only the first page while later pages disclosed third-party access and Ben’s denial of possession. Those later portions did not necessarily prove that Matt wrote the 1:49 p.m. message, but they were necessary to prevent the jury from treating the account name as proof of exclusive control and authorship. Rule 106 permits the adverse party to require contemporaneous introduction of the portions necessary to prevent a misleading impression. Rule 403 separately supports exclusion where the probative value of an isolated page is substantially outweighed by the danger of confusion or misleading the jury. The court offered to allow the defense to introduce the remaining pages. That partially recognized the problem, but it placed the burden of correcting the State’s selective presentation on the defense. The stronger request would have required the State to introduce the necessary context at the same time or forego the isolated page. Best Preserved Objection The Objection That Should Have Been Made Before Admission Authentication, Personal Knowledge, Conditional Relevance, Completeness, and Rule 403 Objection under Rules 104(b), 901(a), 602, 106, and 403, and request for voir dire outside the jury’s presence. The witness has authenticated only that these screenshots appeared on her phone. She has not established personal knowledge that Mr. Allen authored the 1:49 p.m. message. The complete conversation affirmatively shows that another person used the same phone or account, so the displayed name is not sufficient proof of authorship. The Court has conditioned admission on proof of a specific prior bonfire conversation with Mr. Allen, and the State has not supplied that foundation. The State is also attempting to introduce only the first page while omitting the portions showing third-party access and Mr. Allen’s denial of possession. Under Rule 106, the necessary contextual portions must be introduced contemporaneously. Under Rule 403, the isolated page presents a substantial danger of misleading the jury. The defense moves to exclude the exhibit. Alternatively, the defense moves to require the introduction of the complete relevant exchange with an instruction that neither the account name nor admission of the exhibit establishes who authored any particular message. Immediate Objection After the Court’s Reliability Statement N.C. Gen. Stat. § 15A-1222; Curative Instruction; Mistrial if Necessary Objection. The Court’s statement that the exhibit is “sufficiently reliable” expresses an opinion on disputed authorship, credibility, and evidentiary weight, which are questions for the jury under N.C. Gen. Stat. § 15A-1222. The defense requests an immediate instruction that admission of the exhibit does not constitute a finding that Mr. Allen authored any message, that the Court expresses no opinion concerning the exhibit’s reliability or credibility, and that authorship and weight remain solely for the jury. If the prejudice cannot be cured, the defense moves for a mistrial under N.C. Gen. Stat. § 15A-1061. Rules and Professional Duties Authorities Directly Implicated Evidence and Procedure N.C. Gen. records.text: Edifice of Lies Project Map Evidence Viewer Case Record Timeline Players Scene Analysis Evidence Documents Analysis Contradictions 40 Impeachment Cards Deal's Ever Changing Testimony New Face General Videos Inspired Digital Media Case Study Data Snapshot Diagrams Connections False Story Mindmaps Accountability Misconduct Prosecutor Conduct Judicial Duty System Essay Search Soundtrack Scene & Push Dynamics “Crime is contagious. If the government becomes a lawbreaker, it breeds contempt for law.” -Louis Brandeis On this page Overview Bedroom Layout Exhibits Because law enforcement did not conduct a scene analysis, the defense offers the following. The bathroom door leads into an open doorway area that is narrow and confined as it enters the bedroom. Immediately outside of that doorway is a large bed whose mattress is waist height. The bedroom layout creates a short, straight path from the bathroom door to the space beside the bed. There is not enough lateral space for a person to exit the bathroom and simultaneously allow: another adult to stand "behind and to the side," while also having enough angle to create a backward push that sends someone directly backward onto the center of the bed. This spatial reality matters, because her shifting statements require different physical positions that cannot all be true. Physics Major Contradictions Between Her Testimony & The Physical Geometry Direction of Force vs. Direction of Fall • "I was pushed backwards onto his bed." • "I landed on my back." • "He was behind me." • "He was behind me but not directly behind me." • "He pushed me from the side." Physical Reality • A side push does not send someone straight backward onto the bed. • A push from behind-right sends the person diagonally forward-left, not backward. • Falling onto one's back requires a direct backward push from directly in front of or slightly offset but still in front of the person. ➡️ Conclusion: Her described push-angle is not compatible with the resulting body motion she claims. Statement Analysis Contradictions with Interview Statements • "I got grabbed and pushed backwards onto his bed." • "When I went to walk I was pushed backwards." • "He stood in the doorway and told me he was going to watch me." • "I told him to get out… he stood in the doorway." Conflicts: • If he is in the doorway, she cannot "walk out" — he blocks the path. • If he told her he was going to "watch" her from the doorway, it would mean he spoke but she said that he never said a word during her testimony. • If she "walked out," he cannot still be "standing in the doorway. He would have had to move but it is never mentioned. He ends up magically behind her. ➡️ Conclusion: Her statements to law enforcement negate her courtroom version. Position Conflicting Position of the Accused She Testifies: • He was behind me. • He was not directly behind me. • He was to my right and behind me. • He was standing in the doorframe. • He took only "a half step forward." Physical Reality: • The bathroom doorway is narrow. • If he is in the doorframe, he physically blocks her exit. • If she passed him, he cannot be "behind" her without stepping back into the bedroom first, then turning, then pushing. • None of that occurs in her story. ➡️ Conclusion: These arrangements are incompatible with the geometry of the bedroom. Motion Analysis Conflicting Accounts of Her Motion Version 1: "I went to walk out… I got grabbed and pushed backwards onto his bed." Version 2: "He allows you to come out of the bathroom… while he is turned around he pushes you…" Version 3: "He was in the doorway… I made it here… he was here… he took maybe a half step forward and then I got pushed." Physical Reality: • If he is turned around (facing away), he cannot initiate a pushing motion without first rotating. • If he is in the doorway, she cannot exit past him. • If she "made it out," then he is behind her, not in the doorway. • These cannot simultaneously be true. ➡️ Conclusion: Her path of travel and his placement shift in ways that cannot exist in real physical space. Reconstruction Combined Inference (Deductive Reconstruction) A coherent physical reconstruction must satisfy: • Location of persons • Available space • Angle of force • Direction of fall • Final landing position Her story changes each time a physical impossibility is exposed: • When asked if he was behind → she says yes. • When told he couldn't push from there → she says he wasn't "directly" behind. • When shown spatial issues → she moves him to the right. • When told that wouldn't push her backward → she changes to "the side." • When reminded she landed on her back → she reverts to "from behind." ➡️ Conclusion: This pattern is indicative of ad hoc adjustment, not physical memory. Logic Logical Contradictions in Succession 1. He is behind her. 2. He is behind her but not behind enough to push. 3. He is to the right side. 4. He is in the doorway when she passes him but they are both large and they both could not fit in the doorway. 5. He takes only a half-step before pushing. 6. She falls straight backward onto the bed. ➡️ Conclusion: No geometric model or any version of reality satisfies all of these contradictions. Summary of Physical Impossibilities The accuser's testimony contains at least three mutually exclusive descriptions of where the defendant stood and how the push occurred. No single geometric arrangement satisfies all of her claims. This pattern of shifting details—each time adjusting to avoid a newly exposed impossibility—is consistent with fabrication rather than genuine recall of a traumatic event. Bedroom Layout – Claimed Assault Location Lacks sufficient space for two adults in the doorway area Two witnesses outside the window by the fire. An Alexa by the bed that is set to send alerts if anyone says, "I need help." Physical Geometry Exhibits These diagrams visually demonstrate the biomechanical contradictions in her account — specifically, the mismatch between her described push angle, the direction of force, and the backward fall she claims occurred. None of the configurations she provided are compatible with basic physics. ×

records.section: The Failure of the American Justice System
records.text: The Failure of the American Justice System A just system must do two things at once: shield those who are truly in danger and prevent an accusation from becoming punishment before a single fact has been tested. That is not controversial. That is the absolute minimum. Yet our system too often charges in only one direction. An allegation alone becomes a weapon of immediate leverage. Homes are stripped away. Children are turned into bargaining chips. Reputations are demolished. Jobs vanish. Debt piles up like chains. The accused is forced to fight for survival long before the truth is allowed to speak. By the time facts finally matter, the damage is already catastrophic and often irreversible. How It Applies To This Case Project Map Source PDF unavailable
keywords: The Failure of the American Justice System

records.title: Why Don't We Have This System? | State v. Benjamin Allen
records.text: The Greatest Danger The central danger is not merely a false accusation. It is the cold, mechanical conversion of an unproven claim into immediate punishment through process alone. Once that line is crossed, due process ceases to be a living protection. It is reduced to a hollow ritual, something the accused is grudgingly allowed to invoke only after liberty has been seized, housing demolished, family shattered into bargaining chips, money drained to the last dollar, and reputation publicly executed for all to see. The verdict comes later. The sentence has already been served.

records.section: What A Responsible System Would Protect
records.text: What A Responsible System Would Protect Principle 1 Emergency action should not become permanent leverage A functioning system can move quickly in a real emergency without letting temporary measures become automatic punishment. Urgency is not an excuse for vagueness, and caution is not a license to abandon proof. Principle 2 The accused should not be destroyed before a hearing If the consequences are severe, the review must be fast, meaningful, and adversarial. A hearing that comes after the life damage is done is not a safeguard. It is a ritual performed too late. records.text: The Worst Part The worst part is the complete and permanent absence of any testable probable cause documentation, even six years later. There exists only a single magistrate’s order: a skeletal, one-sentence declaration that “sufficient proof existed for an arrest.” No facts. No affidavits. No witness statements. No rationale. Nothing that could ever be subjected to adversarial scrutiny. Six Years An entire life was dismantled without a testable foundation Six years. Six years of a life dismantled: home lost, relationships fractured under relentless stress, children crying through disrupted nights, finances driven into ruin, career erased, and reputation publicly executed, all triggered by an allegation that remains forever shielded from examination. Construction The narrative was built, not discovered The very person tasked with investigating the claim instead helped construct a false narrative to protect its glaring weaknesses. An undisclosed familial conflict turned a preliminary fact-gathering exercise into a prejudicial exercise in insinuation rather than fair investigation. The aggravator was built, not discovered. Freeman’s timeline reveals the matter had already been escalated before the work was even complete. Escalation The state kept strengthening what it never properly grounded Evidence was admitted without device metadata, custodial proof, or any foundational showing that could resolve basic questions of attribution. Witness statements evolved materially between law-enforcement interviews and trial testimony. Social familiarity was strategically reframed into a more legally potent theory. Aggravating exposure increased immediately after the defendant refused a plea, exactly as he had been warned it would. Bottom Line Due process exists on paper and disappears on contact Material witnesses went uninterviewed. Exculpatory inconsistencies were not preserved with candor. Exhibits were framed more forcefully than the underlying record supported. The defense was forced to answer a moving target while the state suppressed or distorted weakening material. The accused is condemned to fight in perpetual darkness while the system that issued the order simply moves on, unaccountable and unexamined. This is not due process. This is due process reduced to a procedural ghost.

Allen | Case No. 19CR 051799 | Lee County, NC Page 1 MEMORANDUM No Remedial Action After Alleged ADA Witness Coaching The Happel Incident, Exhibit 4 Authentication Failures, and the Pattern of Misrepresentations of Evidence to the Court Case: State v. Benjamin Allen | Lee County File No. 19CR 051799 Document Type: Post-Trial Memorandum / Disciplinary Reference Date: July 2026 I. INTRODUCTION AND EXECUTIVE SUMMARY This memorandum addresses a critical and documented failure in the administration of justice in State v. Allen: sworn testimony that Assistant District Attorney Tiffany Bartholomew coached a state witness in the courthouse lobby immediately before trial, and the complete absence of any remedial action by the trial court, the prosecutor’s office, or the North Carolina State Bar. The witness, Steven Happel, reported the incident under oath during a pre-trial colloquy. Despite the gravity of the allegation, the court permitted the trial to proceed without investigation, without curative instruction, without recusal or disqualification of the prosecutor, and without reporting the matter to oversight authorities. The State Bar — which had already received and investigated complaints about Bartholomew in this same case — took no action. The failure to act was not a close call. It was a knowing decision to prioritize trial continuity over witness integrity and prosecutorial ethics. The consequences were immediate and measurable: the complainant’s trial testimony introduced precisely the elements Bartholomew was alleged to have coached — "fear of witnesses" and a "freeze" response — none of which appeared in her 2019 statements to investigators. Forensic linguistic analysis confirms a collapse in narrative consistency (cosine similarity dropping from 1.0 to 0.28) that aligns structurally with the coached transition from situational recall to legalistic element-filling. This memorandum also ties the Happel coaching incident to two other documented failures in the same trial record: (1) the overruling of authentication and hearsay objections to State’s Exhibit 4 — a Facebook message screenshot that the exhibit itself attributed to another user, “Matt," using the Defendant’s phone — and the State’s failure to satisfy the court’s own conditional foundation requirement; and (2) the ADA’s misrepresentation during plea negotiations that sperm evidence had been found, which she later characterized as a “misunderstanding" despite her extensive experience and specialization in sexual assault prosecution. These failures are not isolated. They are branches of the same tree: a prosecution that relied on manufactured evidence, coached testimony, and misrepresentation to sustain a case that the objective record could not support.

records.text: State v. Allen | Case No. 19CR 051799 | Lee County, NC Page 2 II. THE HAPPEL COLLOQUY: THE FACTUAL RECORD On the morning of the trial, before Steven Happel was called to testify, defense counsel brought to the court’s attention that Happel had reported an improper contact with the prosecution team. The court conducted an in-chambers colloquy with Happel, placed him under oath, and took the following sworn account: Sworn Testimony (Steven Happel, Court Colloquy): "I was told to present myself at 2 p.m. yesterday in the old courthouse, and I waited in the lobby. I did go out to my car to kind of relax. I came back in. I talked to the investigator, Scott. I don’t know his last name. I forgot. That’s the only person I talked to about the case, answering questions. And as I was sitting in the main lobby around 2 to 3 p.m. yesterday, Ms. Bartholomew and the victim and other witnesses, maybe, or her family walked in through the front door and were talking about the trial and how the Defendant pleaded or was going to plead, something like that, and then I heard Ms. Bartholomew tell the victim that she should have said that the victim was afraid of the witnesses, which is me and Joseph DeMarco, and I felt intimidated, maybe like my feelings or thought process was trying to be played with, and felt very uncomfortable." Happel further testified that he did not confront Bartholomew at the time, that he believed the incident would affect the trial, and that the ethical question "kind of disturbed” him. The court asked whether he believed the contact would affect his testimony. Happel replied: “The only answers I’ll give are truthful answers that I can recall.” The Court’s Ruling: After the colloquy, the court stated: “I’m satisfied this witness is prepared to tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth, as he indicated under his oath. So we’ll go ahead, then, bring in the jury at this time.” The jury was brought in, and Happel testified directly for the State without any curative instruction, without any investigation of the coaching allegation, and without any sanction or admonishment of ADA Bartholomew. III. WHAT REMEDIAL ACTION WAS REQUIRED The alleged conduct — a prosecutor coaching a witness to claim fear of the defense witnesses — is among the most serious forms of prosecutorial misconduct. It strikes at the heart of the fact-finding process and implicates the Defendant’s due process right to a fair trial. The following remedial options were available and, under controlling authority, required: A. Mistrial or Continuance A trial court has inherent authority to declare a mistrial when prosecutorial misconduct prejudices the Defendant’s right to a fair trial. See N.C. Gen. Stat. §

Where a prosecutor is alleged to have coached a witness, the contamination is not curable by a simple instruction. The witness’s testimony is tainted at its source. A mistrial, or at a minimum a continuance to permit investigation and potential substitution of counsel, was the constitutionally appropriate response. B. Prosecutor Disqualification or Recusal North Carolina courts have the authority to disqualify a prosecutor where conduct violates the rules of professional conduct or deprives the Defendant of a fair trial. See N.C. RPC 3.8 (special responsibilities of a prosecutor); N.C. RPC 8.4 (misconduct). The alleged coaching — directing a witness to fabricate an emotional response to defense witnesses — is precisely the type of conduct that requires disqualification. The trial court took no step to remove Bartholomew from the case or to refer the matter to the district attorney’s office for internal review. C. Curative Instruction Even if the court declined to declare a mistrial or disqualify counsel, it was obligated to provide a curative instruction to the jury. The jury should have been told that an attorney’s attempt to influence witness testimony is improper, that they should scrutinize any testimony that seemed to align with a litigation strategy rather than independent recollection, and that the prosecutor’s conduct was itself evidence of potential witness manipulation. No such instruction was given. D. Investigation and Referral to Oversight Authorities The court was obligated to report the misconduct to the North Carolina State Bar and to the judicial oversight authorities. See N.C. RPC 3.3 (candor toward tribunal); N.C. RPC 8.3 (reporting professional misconduct). The record shows that the State Bar had already received complaints about Bartholomew in this case and had taken no action. The trial court’s failure to report ensured that the disciplinary record remained incomplete and that the Bar’s prior inaction was insulated from correction. IV. THE COURT’S FAILURE TO ACT: A RECONSTRUCTION The trial court’s response to Happel’s sworn allegation can be summarized in three sentences: it held a colloquy, it found Happel credible enough to testify, and it brought the jury in. That is all. There was no investigation, no mistrial, no disqualification, no curative instruction, and no referral to the State Bar. The colloquy itself reveals the inadequacy of the court’s response. The court treated the incident as a credibility question for Happel — “Are you prepared to tell the truth?" — rather than as an ethical crisis requiring structural intervention. This

The question was not whether Happel would tell the truth; the question was whether the State’s case had been manufactured by the prosecutor’s office before the jury ever sat down. The record also shows that the court was aware of the seriousness of the allegation. In chambers, before the colloquy, the court stated that it had been "brought to my attention by the defense attorneys that Mr. Happel may have indicated to them in the last hours that he felt the assistant district attorney prosecuting the case had somehow overstepped her bounds in preparing for trial.” The court’s own language recognized “overstepped her bounds" — yet the remedy was nothing. The trial court’s failure to report the Happel incident left the Bar’s file incomplete. An oversight body that does not investigate cannot discipline; a court that does not report ensures that the oversight body never learns what it must investigate. V. THE CONSEQUENCES: NARRATIVE ENGINEERING VERIFIED The absence of remedial action did not merely leave an allegation unanswered. It permitted the very outcome the coaching was designed to produce: a complainant whose trial testimony incorporated the coached elements with precision. A. The Linguistic Shift Forensic linguistic analysis comparing Lauren Deal’s 2019 statements to investigators with her 2023 trial testimony reveals a dramatic collapse in consistency. The cosine similarity score between her early and late accounts dropped from 1.0 (perfect consistency) to 0.28 (heavily engineered). The shift is not random. It is directional: • She began claiming she "froze" — a term absent from her 2019 interviews and introduced only at trial. • She began invoking "fear of witnesses" — precisely the element Bartholomew was alleged to have coached her to claim. • Her speech register shifted from situational, concrete vocabulary ("truck," "bathroom,” “keys," "firewood") to legalistic, element-filling language ("force," "fear," "trust," "freezing,” “triggers"). This is not natural memory evolution. It is the signature of coached testimony: the witness’s substantive center moves from "what happened" to "what the jury needs to hear to convict." The timing — the shift occurring between 2019 and 2023, with the coached elements first appearing at trial — is consistent with pre-trial preparation rather than delayed disclosure or maturation of recall.

records.text: State v. Allen | Case No. 19CR 051799 | Lee County, NC Page 5 B. Faux Fear The “fear of witnesses” element was not merely linguistically engineered. It was physically implausible. Happel and DeMarco were the defense witnesses. The complainant claimed she was afraid of them. Yet the record shows she was in the same bar, the same vehicle, and the same house with these individuals throughout the evening, initiating contact and social interaction at multiple points. A person who is genuinely afraid of two individuals does not follow them to a house, enter the house alone, and then claim terror as the narrative requires. The coaching supplied the legal vocabulary to paper over this physical inconsistency, and the trial court’s failure to act allowed the jury to hear that vocabulary without context. VI. EXHIBIT 4: AUTHENTICATION FAILURE AND THE COURT’S CONDITIONAL ADMISSION The Happel coaching incident did not occur in isolation. It was part of a broader pattern of evidentiary manipulation that included the State’s handling of Exhibit 4, a December 3, 2016 Facebook message screenshot offered to prove the “position of trust" aggravating factor. The authentication and hearsay problems with Exhibit 4 are directly tied to the same prosecutorial culture that produced the Happel coaching: a willingness to use evidence in ways the record does not support, and to rely on the court’s procedural failures when objections are overruled. A. The Authentication Problem State’s Exhibit 4 was a partial screenshot of Facebook messages. The exhibit’s own content identified the sender as "Matt," who was using the Defendant’s phone. United States (1928) “There is no crueler tyranny than that which is perpetuated under the shield of law and in the name of justice.” Charles de Montesquieu, The Spirit of the Laws (1748) “The true danger inherent in this type of police misconduct is that it subverts the factfinding process itself… The system’s ability to objectively evaluate the evidence is fatally compromised when those charged with gathering it actively manipulate the outcome.” Justice William Brennan, Dissenting in Colorado v. Clark, Majority Opinion in Mapp v. Ohio (1961) “The prosecutor has more control over life, liberty, and reputation than any other person in America. His discretion is tremendous… While the prosecutor at his best is one of the most beneficent forces in our society, when he acts from malice or other base motives, he is one of the worst.” Justice Robert H. Jackson, The Federal Prosecutor (1940) “The United States Attorney is the representative not of an ordinary party to a controversy, but of a sovereignty whose obligation to govern impartially is as compelling as its obligation to govern at all; and whose interest, therefore, in a criminal prosecution is not that it shall win a case, but that justice shall be done. It is as much his duty to refrain from improper methods calculated to produce a wrongful conviction as it is to use every legitimate means to bring about a just one.” Justice George Sutherland, Majority Opinion in Berger v. United States (1935) “The principle that a State may not knowingly use false evidence, including false testimony, to obtain a tainted conviction, implicit in any concept of ordered liberty, does not cease to apply merely because the false testimony goes only to the credibility of the witness. The jury’s estimate of the truthfulness and reliability of a given witness may well be determinative of guilt or innocence, and it is upon such subtle factors as the possible interest of the witness in testifying falsely that a defendant’s life or liberty may depend.” Chief Justice Earl Warren, Majority Opinion in Napue v.
